intro: Revenue per recipient is the average revenue an email campaign generated per email sent. Enter attributed revenue and emails sent to get the figure.

sections.heading: How Revenue per Recipient is calculated
sections.body: Revenue per Recipient = Attributed Revenue ÷ Emails Sent — [the same revenue-over-volume shape used to define revenue per email sent](https://taglab.net/marketing-metrics/revenue-per-email-sent/). Despite the name, this calculator's denominator is every email sent, not a deduplicated count of unique people — see the section below for exactly why that distinction matters.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: $8,000 ÷ 40,000 = $0.20 per email sent. If this same $8,000 came from a smaller list receiving multiple sends during the period, the per-send figure would understate how much revenue each actual person was worth — which is exactly the ambiguity the next section addresses.

sections.heading: "Recipient" here means every send, not every unique person
sections.body: This is the one detail worth getting right before using the number. [Some sources define "revenue per recipient" with a denominator of unique recipients — counting each person once even if they received multiple emails during the period](https://count.co/metric/email-revenue-per-recipient) — while this calculator's own "emails sent" input counts every send, including repeat sends to the same person. If a list of 10,000 people received 4 emails each during a period, this calculator's denominator would be 40,000, not 10,000. That's not a bug — it matches the specific inputs this calculator asks for — but it means a result computed here isn't directly comparable to a unique-recipient version of the same-named metric pulled from another source without accounting for send frequency.

sections.heading: Revenue per Recipient vs. Revenue per Visitor
sections.body: Both express "how much revenue per unit of audience reached," but from different channels and different denominators. Revenue per Recipient divides email-attributed revenue by emails sent — a channel-specific figure scoped to one campaign or one sending period. [Revenue per Visitor](/calculators/revenue-per-visitor) divides site-wide revenue by site visitors, covering every traffic source at once, not just email. A strong Revenue per Recipient figure doesn't automatically mean a strong Revenue per Visitor figure, and the two shouldn't be added or averaged together — they're measuring related but structurally different slices of the same business.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Comparing this calculator's per-send result against a unique-recipient-denominator figure from another source without adjusting for send frequency first.
Attributing revenue from unrelated channels (paid search, organic, direct) to email, inflating the numerator beyond what email actually drove.
Mixing a revenue figure from one time period with an emails-sent count from a different period.
Treating a single high-revenue campaign (a major sale, a product launch) as the typical, ongoing per-recipient figure rather than an outlier worth reporting separately.

faq.a: Revenue per recipient is the average revenue an email campaign generated for every email sent, calculated as attributed revenue divided by emails sent. It's one of the more direct ways to connect email marketing activity to actual business results, rather than stopping at engagement metrics like open rate or click-through rate that don't confirm any revenue was produced. This calculator's denominator counts every email sent, including repeat sends to the same person during the measurement period — it does not deduplicate down to unique individuals, which is a real distinction worth understanding before comparing this figure against other sources. Tracking it alongside a revenue-neutral engagement metric like open rate helps separate a genuine revenue problem from a simple reach problem.

faq.q: How do you calculate Revenue per Recipient?
faq.a: Divide attributed revenue by emails sent: Revenue per Recipient = Revenue ÷ Emails Sent. A campaign that generated $8,000 in attributed revenue from 40,000 emails sent has a revenue per recipient of $8,000 ÷ 40,000 = $0.20. Both figures need to come from the same campaign or sending period, and the revenue figure should reflect only sales genuinely attributable to that email activity — mixing in revenue from unrelated channels inflates the result and misrepresents what the email campaign actually drove. Most email platforms with revenue tracking calculate this automatically once purchase events are connected to campaign sends, so it's usually available as a report rather than something computed by hand from raw logs.

faq.q: Does "recipient" mean unique people or total emails sent?
faq.a: In this calculator, it means total emails sent, not unique people. That's worth flagging because other sources define "revenue per recipient" with a unique-recipient denominator, counting each person once regardless of how many emails they received during the period. If a list of 10,000 people each received 4 emails, this calculator's denominator would be 40,000, while a unique-recipient version of the metric would use 10,000 — a fourfold difference in the result. Neither approach is wrong, but they answer slightly different questions, and the two shouldn't be compared directly without adjusting for send frequency. Checking which denominator a specific report or benchmark used before treating two figures as comparable avoids a mismatch that can look like a real performance difference.

faq.q: What counts as "attributed revenue" in this calculation?
faq.a: Attributed revenue should be limited to sales that can reasonably be tied to the specific email campaign or sending period being measured — typically purchases made through a tracked link in the email, within whatever attribution window the sending platform uses. Revenue from other channels, or purchases with no connection to the email at all, shouldn't be included, since that inflates the result and overstates what the email activity actually produced. Attribution methodology varies by platform and business, so the specific window and rules used should stay consistent across periods being compared. A common attribution window is 24 to 72 hours after a click, though the exact length is a platform or business decision, not a fixed industry standard.

faq.q: What is a good Revenue per Recipient figure?
faq.a: There's no universal good figure — it depends heavily on average order value, product price point, industry, and list quality, all of which shift the number independent of how well the email program is actually performing. A high-ticket B2B product will naturally produce a very different revenue-per-recipient figure than a low-cost consumer good, without either representing better email marketing. This figure is most useful tracked against a business's own history over time, using a consistent attribution methodology and denominator definition, rather than compared against an outside benchmark pulled from a different context. A sudden drop worth investigating is more informative than a static number compared to an unrelated business's published average.
